steps: Step 1, Explain development. Development means people live longer, healthier, better-educated lives, not only that a country earns more. Income per person is one measure: a country with a GDP of 3,000 billion and 1,500 million people has 3,000 billion divided by 1,500 million, which is 2,000 per person.

Step 2, Explain why averages can hide gaps. If 2,000 is the average but a few people earn most of the income, many families live far below it. So economists also look at life expectancy, years of schooling and the share of people in poverty, not income alone.

Step 3, Explain money and credit. Money works as a medium of exchange and a store of value. Credit is a loan repaid later with interest. Borrow 10,000 at 8 percent a year for 3 years: simple interest gives 12,400 back, but yearly compounding gives 10,000 times 1.08 cubed, which is 12,597.12.

Step 4, Explain who gains and loses from credit. Formal credit from a bank at 8 percent can help a farmer buy seed and raise output. A moneylender charging far higher interest can trap a borrower in debt. Cheap, fair credit supports development; costly credit can undo it.

Step 5, Explain globalisation and trade. Globalisation links markets through trade, investment and technology. If 1 unit of a foreign currency costs 80 of ours, a 25-unit foreign import costs 2,000 of ours. Trade gives choice and larger markets, but can hurt small producers who cannot match imported prices.

Step 6, Your turn: a loan of 5,000 at 10 percent compounded yearly for 2 years is taken by a small shop. How much is owed, and name one gain and one risk of imports. Answer: 5,000 times 1.1 squared is 6,050; gain is cheaper choice, risk is competition for local makers.

Step 1, Listen to a short story. Tom runs in the hall and bumps a cup. It falls and breaks. Nobody saw it. Tom's tummy feels tight and his face feels hot. Ask the child: how do you think Tom feels? Scared and a little worried.
Step 2, Name the two choices. Tom can say, 'It was not me,' or he can say, 'I broke it. I am sorry.' The first is a lie, which is not true. The second is the truth, which tells what really happened.

Step 3, Tell the truth in the story. Tom walks to his teacher and says, 'I ran and I broke the cup. I am sorry.' Say the sentence slowly together. Use plain words: what I did, and sorry. Do not blame a friend.

Step 4, Say how it feels. After Tom tells the truth, his tummy feels loose and light. He feels relieved, which means the heavy worry is gone. The teacher says, 'Thank you for telling me,' and helps him pick up the pieces safely.

Step 5, Notice that telling the truth can be hard but helps. A lie can make a worry grow bigger, like a snowball. Truth lets people fix the problem together. Count the feelings in the story: scared, relieved, proud. That is 3 feelings.

Step 6, Your turn: Mia spills juice on the floor and nobody sees. Tell the true thing she can say and how she will feel after. Answer: 'I spilled the juice, please may I have a cloth?' She will feel relieved and proud.

Step 1, Learn four polite words. Please is for asking, thank you is for when we get something, sorry is for when we hurt someone, and excuse me is for getting past or getting attention. Say each word aloud and clap once for each.
Step 2, Put the words in a sentence. 'Please may I have a pencil?' 'Thank you for the pencil.' 'Sorry I bumped your arm.' 'Excuse me, may I get past?' Say them in a kind voice with a smile.

Step 3, Learn to listen. Listening has four parts: eyes look at the speaker, ears hear, mouth stays quiet, and hands stay still. Count the four parts on your fingers. Practise while a friend tells you one short sentence.

Step 4, Wait for a turn. Mia is talking. Sam wants to speak too. Sam raises his hand and waits until Mia finishes. Then Sam says, 'Excuse me, may I tell you something?' Waiting shows Mia that her words matter.

Step 5, Notice how it feels. When someone says please, you feel respected. When someone talks over you, you may feel sad. Polite words and good listening make people feel safe and happy. Say one way you were polite today.

Step 6, Your turn: you want a drink of water at the table. Say two polite words you will use, and say what you do while a friend is talking. Answer: please and thank you; I look, listen and wait quietly.

Step 1, Learn that water is precious. We drink it, wash with it and grow food with it. A tap left running while you brush teeth for 2 minutes can use about 6 litres each minute, so about 12 litres. That is 12 big one-litre bottles.

Step 2, Choose a small water-saving action. Turn the tap off while brushing, and turn it on only to rinse. Use a cup of about a quarter of a litre to rinse. Now you use far less than 12 litres, and the water is saved.
Step 3, Count the saving across a week. If you save about 12 litres each day by turning off the tap, in 7 days you save 12 times 7, which is 84 litres. Draw 7 drops, one for each day you remembered.

Step 4, Learn about waste. Waste is rubbish we throw away. Small actions reduce it: use both sides of paper, bring a refillable bottle, and put litter in a bin. Never pick up broken glass or sharp things; ask an adult.

Step 5, Match an action to a reason. Turn off the tap, so water is not wasted. Use both sides of paper, so fewer trees are cut. Bin your litter, so animals and playgrounds stay clean. Say the reason after each action.

Step 6, Your turn: choose one action to save water and one to reduce waste at home, and give a reason for each. Answer: I turn off the tap while brushing so water is saved; I draw on both sides of paper so I use less.

Step 1, Learn that gifts are not only things. A gift can be a toy, but also a kind friend, a good meal, a clean park, or a talent like singing. Draw one gift you have that is not something you bought.
Step 2, Learn what gratitude means. Gratitude is feeling thankful and showing it. When someone gives you a gift or helps you, you can say, 'Thank you for helping me.' Say it with eyes up and a smile.

Step 3, Practise thank-you sentences with a reason. 'Thank you, Grandma, for cooking dinner.' 'Thank you, teacher, for helping me read.' Adding the reason shows you noticed what the person did, and that makes the thanks feel real.

Step 4, Make a gratitude list. Name three things you are grateful for today: for example my family, clean water and my friend. If you list 3 things a day for 5 days, you will have 15 things. Write or draw them.

Step 5, Notice how it feels. When you say thank you, the other person feels happy and so do you. Gratitude can turn a bad day around because it helps you look at what is good, not only what is missing.

Step 6, Your turn: write one thank-you sentence to a person who helped you this week and name two things you are grateful for. Answer: 'Thank you, Dad, for helping with my bag.' I am grateful for my friends and my home.

Step 1, Describe a mistake. A mistake is something that went wrong when we were learning or trying. Example: Sam took a spelling test of 10 words and got 6 right. He wrote 'becuase' instead of 'because'. That is what happened.

Step 2, Find why it happened. Sam hurried and did not check the order of letters. Asking why helps us learn. We do not say 'I am bad at spelling'; we say, 'I did not check my word, so next time I will.'

Step 3, Say what was learned. Sam learned that 'because' is spelled b-e-c-a-u-s-e, and that checking each word takes only a few seconds. A good sentence has three parts: what happened, what I learned, and what I will do next.
Step 4, Make a plan to improve. Sam writes the 4 wrong words on cards and practises 5 minutes each day. After 4 days he tries again. A mistake is a chance to grow, as long as we try again.

Step 5, Check the progress. In the next test Sam gets 8 out of 10. That is 2 more than 6, so he improved by 2 marks. He feels proud because his effort made a difference, not because he never made a mistake.

Step 6, Your turn: describe a mistake of your own in three short sentences: what happened, what you learned, and what you will do. Answer: I spilled paint because I rushed; I learned to go slowly; next time I will hold the cup with two hands.
Step 1, Learn the three Rs. Reduce means use less. Reuse means use again. Recycle means turn old things into new things. They work in that order: first reduce, then reuse, then recycle what is left.

Step 2, Choose a reduce action. Carry a refillable water bottle. If a family uses 4 plastic bottles each week, that is 4 times 52, which is 208 bottles a year. A refillable bottle cuts that number a lot.

Step 3, Choose a reuse action. Wash an empty jar and use it as a pencil holder. Use old cardboard boxes for storage. Keep a bag to carry shopping again and again. Ask an adult to handle any broken glass.

Step 4, Choose a recycle action. Put clean paper, card, metal tins and glass in the recycling bin where your town collects them. Rinse them first and keep them separate from food waste, so they can be made into new items.

Step 5, Sort five items. A used notebook page: reuse by drawing on the back. A banana peel: compost. A plastic bottle: reduce by choosing a refillable one, or recycle. An old toy: reuse by giving it to a friend. Explain each choice.

Step 6, Your turn: pick one reduce, one reuse and one recycle action you can do this week. Answer: reduce by bringing a refillable bottle, reuse a jar for pencils, recycle clean paper in the paper bin.

Step 1, Explain what trust is. Trust means believing that a person will be honest and do what they say. Imagine a friend who promises to return your book in 3 days and does. You start to trust that friend a little more.

Step 2, Explain why trust takes time. Trust grows from many small actions, not one big one. If a person keeps 5 promises each week for 4 weeks, that is 20 kept promises. Each one adds a small piece, like laying bricks.

Step 3, Explain how trust breaks quickly. One lie can undo many kept promises, because it makes people wonder what else is untrue. Building a wall takes many bricks; knocking it down can take one push.

Step 4, Explain how to rebuild trust. Admit what happened, say sorry, make it right, and then keep your promises again over time. Example: Hamza breaks a game, tells the truth, and offers to help repair it. Trust returns slowly.

Step 5, Explain with a short example. A student who is always on time, tells the truth about homework and keeps secrets will be trusted with more jobs, like class monitor. Trust is earned by steady behaviour, not by words alone.

Step 6, Your turn: explain in two sentences why a friend who has told 1 lie will need more than 1 day to be trusted again. Answer: one honest day is a small sign; trust grows only when many actions over time show the person can be relied on.
Step 1, Learn what perseverance means. It means to keep trying even when something is hard or slow. A learner on a bike falls, gets up and tries again. Each try teaches the body something new.

Step 2, Set a small goal. A good goal is clear, small and has a time. Example: 'I will learn 12 spelling words in 4 days.' That means 12 divided by 4, which is 3 new words each day, an easy daily step.
Step 3, Plan the steps. Day 1: words 1 to 3. Day 2: words 4 to 6. Day 3: words 7 to 9. Day 4: words 10 to 12. Write them on a chart and tick each day. Seeing ticks helps you keep going.
Step 4, Meet a problem and keep trying. On day 2 you forget two words. Do not quit. Say, 'I have not learned them yet.' Practise them again, write them 3 times each, and ask a friend to test you.
Step 5, Check the result. After 4 days you test yourself and get 11 of 12 right. That is not perfect, but it is a big step. Celebrate effort, then set the next small goal for the one word you missed.

Step 6, Your turn: set a small goal to read a 24-page story in 4 days and say how many pages per day. Answer: 24 divided by 4 is 6 pages each day; if I miss a day, I read 12 pages the next day and keep going.

Step 1, Describe how people differ. People can differ in looks, language, food, clothes, family type, age, abilities and interests. Look around the class and name three differences, such as height, favourite sport and the language spoken at home.

Step 2, Describe how people are equal. Equal means everyone deserves fair treatment, respect and the same basic rights, like a safe place to learn. Being different does not make one person worth more or less than another.

Step 3, Learn from a table. Ana speaks two languages, Ben uses a wheelchair, and Chen loves chess. Each has different needs and skills. All three should be allowed to play, learn and speak, so we make space for each one.

Step 4, Notice unfair talk. Calling someone names for how they look or speak is unkind and untrue. A fair response is to say, 'Please stop,' include the person, and tell a trusted adult if it continues.

Step 5, Show respect through actions. Ask a friend to teach you a word in their home language, make a ramp or space for a wheelchair, and offer a game where everyone can join. Count the actions: that is 3 ways to include others.

Step 6, Your turn: describe in one sentence how two classmates can be different and equal. Answer: one may speak Hindi at home and the other English, but both deserve the same respect and the same chance to learn.

Step 1, Learn what empathy means. Empathy is understanding what another person feels and thinks by imagining being in their place. It is different from sympathy, which is feeling sorry from outside. Empathy asks, 'What is it like for you?'

Step 2, Read a situation. Lina joins a new school in the middle of term. At break she sits alone and holds her lunch box. Several children are playing a ball game nearby, and no one has invited her yet.

Step 3, View it from Lina's side. She may feel nervous, lonely and shy. She may think, 'Nobody wants me.' Use feeling words: worried, left out, hopeful. Her silence does not mean she dislikes the others; she may be waiting to be asked.

Step 4, View it from a classmate's side. A classmate may think, 'She looks like she wants to be alone,' or may not have noticed her. They are not bad people; they just see a different part of the story. That is why a view changes with the viewer.
Step 5, Write an empathy sentence. Use this frame: 'I think you feel ___ because ___, so I could ___.' Example: 'I think you feel left out because you are new, so I could ask you to join our game.'

Step 6, Your turn: a friend gets a low mark and goes quiet. Write an empathy sentence from their view. Answer: 'I think you feel disappointed because you worked hard, so I could sit with you and offer to study together.'

Step 1, Define integrity. Integrity means doing what is right even when no one is watching, and your words match your actions. Honesty is part of it. Read the case: a shop gives a student 50 in change when it should be 30.

Step 2, Ask what is going on. Who is affected? The shopkeeper loses 20 and the student gains 20 by mistake, since 50 minus 30 is 20. The student has noticed and nobody else has. The facts matter before the choice.

Step 3, List the options. One: keep the extra 20 and say nothing. Two: say 'You gave me too much change' and return it. Three: pretend not to notice and leave. Write each option and who is helped or harmed by it.

Step 4, Test each option. Would you be happy if someone did this to you? Would you be comfortable if your family knew? Keeping the money fails both tests. Returning it passes. A good test is also whether you could say your choice aloud.

Step 5, Decide and give a reason. The right choice is to return the extra 20, because it is not yours and keeping it harms someone who worked for it. Doing the right thing can be uncomfortable, but it builds trust and self-respect.

Step 6, Your turn: you find a classmate's purse with 15 inside and nobody sees you. Decide what is right and give a reason. Answer: hand it to the teacher with the money still in it, because it belongs to the classmate.

Step 1, Describe respect. Respect means treating people as valuable, listening, and not mocking. It applies to every person whatever their culture, language or ability. A simple rule is to treat others as you would like to be treated.

Step 2, Notice cultural differences. People greet in different ways: 'Hola' in Spanish, 'Bonjour' in French, 'Jambo' in Swahili and 'Konnichiwa' in Japanese all mean a form of hello. Learning a greeting shows interest and respect.

Step 3, Notice that customs differ. Some cultures bow, some shake hands, some place a hand on the chest. None is better or worse. Before judging, ask, 'Why do you do it this way?' Curiosity is respectful; ridicule is not.

Step 4, Describe respect for abilities. About 1 in 6 people in the world live with a significant disability. Ramps help wheelchair users, braille helps blind readers, and sign language helps deaf people. Respect includes making places and activities accessible.

Step 5, Use respectful words. Say 'a person who uses a wheelchair', not a word that defines someone only by a condition. Ask before helping, and speak to the person, not about them. Check you understand by listening first.

Step 6, Your turn: describe in two sentences one way to show respect to a new classmate who speaks another language and one who uses crutches. Answer: learn a greeting in their language; hold the door and ask if they want help.

Step 1, Plan the measurement. For 7 days, collect the household waste in one bag. Use gloves, wash your hands afterwards and never touch sharp items or food scraps; ask an adult to handle those. Weigh the bag on a kitchen scale each evening.

Step 2, Record the results. Suppose the family of 4 produces 3.5 kg in 7 days. Per person per week that is 3.5 divided by 4, which is 0.875 kg. Per person per day it is 3,500 grams divided by 28 person-days, which is 125 grams.

Step 3, Sort the waste. Split it into food, paper, plastic, metal or glass, and other. Weigh each pile and write it in a table. Work out each share: for example 1.4 kg of food waste is 1.4 divided by 3.5, which is 40 percent.

Step 4, Choose reduction actions. Plan meals to cut food waste, use a refillable bottle, take a cloth bag to the shop, compost peelings and recycle clean paper. Pick two actions that target the biggest pile, because they save the most.

Step 5, Measure again and compare. If a second week gives 2.8 kg, that is 3.5 minus 2.8, which is 0.7 kg less. The reduction is 0.7 divided by 3.5, which is 20 percent. Report the change in a short chart.
Step 6, Your turn: a home had 5 kg of waste in week 1 and 4 kg in week 2. Find the percentage reduction. Answer: 1 kg less, 1 divided by 5 is 20 percent, so waste fell by 20 percent.

Step 1, Find your time budget. A week has 7 times 24, which is 168 hours. Sleep at 8 hours a night takes 56 hours and school at 6 hours on 5 days takes 30. That leaves 82 hours for meals, family, study, sport, hobbies and screens.

Step 2, Track current screen use. Check the device's usage report for a week, or tally it in a notebook. Separate learning use from leisure use. Be honest about the total; a plan only works when it starts from real numbers.

Step 3, Set limits. Plan 2 hours of leisure screen time on 5 school days and 3 hours on 2 weekend days. That is 10 plus 6, which is 16 hours. As a share of the week, 16 divided by 168 is about 9.5 percent.

Step 4, Protect sleep and eyes. Stop screens about an hour before bed and keep the phone out of the bedroom overnight. Use the 20-20-20 habit: every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet (about 6 metres) away for 20 seconds.

Step 5, Add balanced alternatives. Plan time for exercise, face-to-face friends, reading and hobbies. Write the weekly plan in a table with days across the top, and review after 2 weeks to see whether it feels realistic.

Step 6, Your turn: plan screen time of 1.5 hours on 5 weekdays and 2.5 hours on 2 weekend days, and find the weekly total. Answer: 1.5 times 5 is 7.5, plus 2.5 times 2 which is 5, so the total is 12.5 hours.

Step 1, Describe values. Values are the beliefs that matter most to a person, such as honesty, kindness, fairness, courage and responsibility. They act like an inner compass when choices are hard. Write down five values you care about.

Step 2, Rank your values. Put the five in order, from the most to the least important to you. Ranking is hard because values can conflict, such as honesty with a friend and kindness to a friend. Your top three guide most decisions.

Step 3, Link values to a case. You find a wallet with 20 in cash and a student card. If honesty ranks high, you return it. If fairness ranks high, you think how you would feel if it were yours. Values point to the same action.

Step 4, See what character is. Character is the pattern of how you act, built by repeating choices. Returning the wallet once is an act; doing the right thing again and again makes it part of who you are.

Step 5, Describe values when they conflict. A friend asks you to keep a secret that could harm them. Honesty and loyalty clash. Weigh the harm: safety usually comes first, so you tell a trusted adult and explain why with care.

Step 6, Your turn: pick one value and describe in two sentences how it guided a recent choice. Answer: I valued honesty, so I admitted I had not finished my work, and that let my teacher help me catch up.

Step 1, Name stress signs. Stress is the body's response to pressure. Body signs include a fast heartbeat, headaches, tight muscles and poor sleep. Feeling signs include worry, irritability and feeling overwhelmed. List three signs you notice in yourself.

Step 2, Know that stress can be useful. A little stress before a test can help focus. It becomes a problem when it lasts for weeks or stops you from sleeping, eating or enjoying things. Time and strength of stress matter.

Step 3, Learn a breathing skill. Box breathing: breathe in for 4 seconds, hold 4, breathe out 4, hold 4. One round takes 16 seconds, so 4 rounds take 64 seconds. Do it sitting, and stop if you feel dizzy.
Step 4, Learn more coping skills. Move your body, sleep 8 to 10 hours, break big tasks into small steps, limit news and screens, and talk with someone you trust. Pick two skills that suit you.

Step 5, Know when to ask for help. If stress or low mood lasts more than two weeks, or you feel unsafe, speak to a parent, teacher, school counsellor or doctor. Asking for help is a strength. Resilience means recovering, and it grows with support.

Step 6, Your turn: name two stress signs before exams and two coping skills you could use this week. Answer: fast heartbeat and poor sleep; box breathing for 4 rounds and a 20-minute walk each evening.

Step 1, Count the hours. A week has 168 hours. Write the fixed items first: school and travel 35 hours, sleep 9 hours a night which is 63, and meals and chores about 2 hours a day, which is 14. Fixed time is 35 plus 63 plus 14, which is 112.

Step 2, Add study and exercise. Plan 2 hours of study on 5 weekdays and 1 hour on each weekend day, giving 10 plus 2, which is 12 hours. Add 5 hours of exercise. Study and exercise take 17 hours in total.

Step 3, Find rest time. 168 minus 35, 63, 14, 12 and 5 leaves 39 hours for friends, family, hobbies and unplanned rest. That is about 5.6 hours a day. Rest is not wasted time; it helps memory and mood.
Step 4, Build the timetable. Put study in 25 to 50 minute blocks with 5 to 10 minute breaks. Do hard subjects when you are alert. Keep a regular bedtime, and keep one evening a week free from study.
Step 5, Review and adjust. After a week, mark what worked, what ran over and when you were tired. Move or shorten tasks. A routine is a plan you test, not a rule you must keep perfectly.

Step 6, Your turn: if sleep rises to 8 hours a night, how many hours does a week of sleep take, and what is left from 168 after school 35, sleep and 14 meals? Answer: 56 hours of sleep; 168 minus 35, 56 and 14 leaves 63.

Step 1, Learn three lenses. Consequences asks which choice gives the best result for the people affected. Duties asks which rules or promises must be kept. Character asks what an honest, fair, caring person would do. Use all three on a case before you decide.

Step 2, Read a commerce case. A firm has made 50,000 units of a product and finds a defect that harms 1 in 2,000 users. Expected harm is 50,000 divided by 2,000, which is 25 people. A recall would cost the firm a large sum, and it could lose profit and customers.

Step 3, Apply consequences. Recall: avoids about 25 injuries and protects the firm's reputation over time, though it costs money now. Say nothing: saves cost now but risks injury, legal penalties and lost trust later. Compare short-term and long-term effects.

Step 4, Apply duties and character. The firm has a duty to sell safe goods, to be honest with customers and to follow product-safety law. A fair, honest business leader would warn users and fix the problem, even at a price.

Step 5, Decide and justify. Write: 'The firm should recall, because the consequences, duties and character lenses agree.' Then name a cost and how to reduce it, such as refunds and clear notices. Wellbeing also matters; people who act ethically often sleep better.

Step 6, Your turn: a seller knows a battery overheats in 1 of 500 units out of 10,000 sold. Find the expected number of faulty units and say what to do. Answer: 10,000 divided by 500 is 20 units; warn buyers and recall them.

Step 1, Learn three lenses. Consequences asks which choice produces the most good for the people affected. Duties asks which rules, rights or promises must be respected. Character asks what a fair, honest, caring person would do. Use all three before you decide.

Step 2, Read a humanities case. A town council has 120,000 to spend. A footbridge repair serves 900 people a week, including children walking to school. A youth centre serves 150 people a week. Cost per weekly user is 120,000 divided by 900, about 133, for the bridge.

Step 3, Apply consequences. The bridge helps 900 weekly users, which is 6 times as many as the 150 the youth centre helps. A damaged bridge may also cause accidents. The centre would help a smaller group, though possibly with deeper benefit. Compare size and depth of benefit.

Step 4, Apply duties and character. A council has a duty to keep public routes safe and to treat all groups fairly, including young people. A fair leader would listen to both groups, explain the choice openly and look for other funds for the centre.

Step 5, Decide and justify. Write: 'The council should repair the bridge first, because safety and benefit to the greatest number matter, and then seek funds for the centre.' Note the weakness: it leaves a smaller group waiting, so give a clear timeline.

Step 6, Your turn: a library can open late either for 300 students a week or for 60 adults on a night shift. Which lens gives which answer? Answer: consequences favours 300 students, duty to serve all fairly suggests a mix, character suggests listening to both groups.

Step 1, Learn three lenses. Consequences asks which choice gives the best result for the people affected. Duties asks which rules or promises, such as honest reporting, must be kept. Character asks what an honest, careful scientist would do. Use all three on a case.

Step 2, Read a science case. A student records 10 readings: 9.8, 9.7, 9.9, 9.8, 9.6, 9.7, 9.8, 12.4, 9.9, 9.7. The mean is 100.3 divided by 10, which is 10.03. Without 12.4 it is 9.77. The student wonders about deleting the odd value quietly.

Step 3, Apply consequences. Hiding the value makes the result look cleaner but may mislead readers and later work. Keeping it and saying it may be an error is honest and lets others judge. Short-term neatness costs long-term trust in the result.

Step 4, Apply duties and character. A scientist has a duty to report data truthfully, to give a reason for any exclusion and to keep the original record. A careful, honest person would check the instrument, repeat the reading and report both versions.

Step 5, Decide and justify. Write: 'Report all 10 readings, mark 12.4 as a possible outlier, and give both means with a reason.' The median is 9.8 either way, which is useful because it hardly changes. Doing this protects your wellbeing too, since nothing needs hiding.

Step 6, Your turn: readings 4.1, 4.0, 4.2, 4.1 and 6.0 add up to 22.4. Find the mean and say what to do with 6.0. Answer: the mean is 4.48; keep 6.0 in the record, flag it, check the instrument and report with and without it.
